open_codes.label: DHT-backed Git object storage
open_codes.rationale: The document describes storing content-addressed Git objects in a distributed hash table as an object-level scaling design. Although it supported normal Git operations, the design was ultimately discarded because Git clone still required packfiles over the network and performed poorly.

open_codes.label: Custom JGit storage abstraction
open_codes.rationale: JGit supplied the interfaces and factories needed to replace ordinary on-disk packfiles with a distributed hash table, making the DHT-backed design technically possible.

open_codes.label: Sequential DAG traversal over distributed storage
open_codes.rationale: Git operations must walk commits, trees, files, subtrees, and parent pointers step by step; the next object key is unknown until the previous object is fetched, creating repeated remote dependencies.

open_codes.label: Distributed-store round-trip amplification
open_codes.rationale: When each step of a Git DAG walk requires a round trip to a distributed store, even simple repository operations become increasingly expensive at scale.

open_codes.label: Git-protocol packfile transfer requirement
open_codes.rationale: The document identifies a protocol constraint: Git sends packfiles over the network during cloning regardless of how objects are stored on the server, limiting the benefits of object-level distribution.

open_codes.label: Poor clone performance
open_codes.rationale: The DHT-based implementation achieved results good enough for normal Git operations, but its clone performance was bad enough that the overall design was discarded.

open_codes.label: WAL-based repository storage
open_codes.rationale: The system adopts a write-ahead-log architecture as an alternative to depending on an external relational database for Git references or object data. The choice is driven by prioritizing Git-data consistency over operational simplicity and database transaction scalability.

open_codes.label: External relational database dependency
open_codes.rationale: A design using blob storage for packfiles and a relational database for references is explicitly described as an alternative that the team declined, because operating an external database and synchronizing repository state would weaken the preferred consistency model.

open_codes.label: WAL durability before push acknowledgement
open_codes.rationale: Pushes are not acknowledged until the complete operation has been persisted to the WAL, making durable logging the acceptance point for client-visible repository changes.

open_codes.label: Linearized push processing
open_codes.rationale: The system linearizes all pushes rather than allowing concurrent push effects to form an ambiguous ordering, supporting consistent repository states and traceable operation history.

open_codes.label: Fully consistent repository views
open_codes.rationale: Every accessed repository view is maintained as fully consistent, avoiding partially applied or divergent views in a system exposed to corruption, repacking bugs, and push races.

open_codes.label: Complete WAL provenance for repository operations
open_codes.rationale: Fundamental repository operations, including pushes and repacks, are recorded in the WAL so that every historical repository state can be inspected and replicas can be rewound or fast-forwarded.

open_codes.label: On-disk Git repository with standard Git tooling
open_codes.rationale: Git operations continue to run on a normal repository on disk using off-the-shelf Git tooling, rather than introducing a specialized implementation; this limits the number of new bugs added to the system.

open_codes.label: Immediate reboot for planned maintenance
open_codes.rationale: Directly rebooting or unplugging a server is explicitly described as an overly disruptive approach because it breaks in-progress reads, especially long-running repository clones.

open_codes.label: Quiescing period before server reboot
open_codes.rationale: Planned reboots begin by marking the server offline for new reads while allowing existing operations to complete, reusing failure-handling logic without interrupting long-running clients.

open_codes.label: Read admission exclusion during quiescing
open_codes.rationale: While quiescing, the server is excluded from new read operations so newly started requests do not become dependent on a server that is about to shut down.

open_codes.label: Completion of in-progress reads during quiescing
open_codes.rationale: Existing reads, including clones of large repositories, are allowed to finish before shutdown to avoid losing potentially hours of client progress.

open_codes.label: Continued write replication during quiescing
open_codes.rationale: Writes continue to be sent to the quiescing server because writes run on all replicas and stopping them would let that replica fall arbitrarily far behind.

open_codes.label: Replica voting without the rebooting server
open_codes.rationale: In-progress writes can proceed because the other two replicas can vote without the server being rebooted, preserving write availability during maintenance.

open_codes.label: Interrupted clone progress loss
open_codes.rationale: Breaking a long-running read such as a large-repository clone forces a restart on another replica and loses all progress made up to interruption.

open_codes.label: Quiescing duration variability
open_codes.rationale: The maintenance delay varies from seconds to many hours depending on the long-running reads active on the server.

open_codes.label: Per-application-server file-server failure detection
open_codes.rationale: Failure detectors operate across each application server and each file server, so a resolver failure on one application server produces a localized, rather than system-wide, view of file-server availability.

open_codes.label: Three-copy repository replication
open_codes.rationale: Spokes keeps at least three copies of every repository, wiki, and gist to preserve repository data through server, disk, rack, or controller failures.

open_codes.label: Cross-rack replica placement
open_codes.rationale: Replicas are placed in different racks, protecting repository data against failure of an entire rack rather than only an individual node.

open_codes.label: Strict-majority write acceptance
open_codes.rationale: Repository updates are accepted only when a strict majority of replicas applies the change and obtains the same result, supporting durable and consistent updates.

open_codes.label: Single-extra-copy durability strategy
open_codes.rationale: The document notes that one additional copy would be sufficient to survive a single-node failure, but this option does not provide the majority-based coordination needed for conflicting concurrent writes.

open_codes.label: Majority-held exclusive write locks
open_codes.rationale: Each write acquires an exclusive lock on a majority of replicas, preventing two conflicting writes from acquiring a majority simultaneously.

open_codes.label: Replica-wide write serialization
open_codes.rationale: Conflicting writes are applied or rejected in the same order on every replica, ensuring that replicas converge on the same result.

open_codes.label: Localized impact of a faulty application server
open_codes.rationale: When one staging application server lost DNS resolution, its incorrect offline determinations were isolated to that server; other application servers continued normally and production traffic was unaffected.

open_codes.label: Periodic repository compaction
open_codes.rationale: The document treats compaction as necessary because unbounded WAL growth makes full restores increasingly expensive and accumulating Git packfiles makes object lookup inefficient.

open_codes.label: Primary-only compaction
open_codes.rationale: The system assigns compaction work only to the primary replica, avoiding concurrent maintenance operations across multiple Spokes nodes for the same repository.

open_codes.label: Coupled disk-repository and WAL compaction
open_codes.rationale: The compaction result is applied to both the on-disk Git repository and the write-ahead log, keeping the persisted repository and replication stream aligned.

open_codes.label: WAL-propagated compaction events
open_codes.rationale: Replicas follow compaction events through the WAL, allowing the primary to coordinate repository maintenance without having every replica independently perform the operation.

open_codes.label: Replica-side repacking
open_codes.rationale: Replicas do not repack repositories themselves; the document explicitly describes avoiding replica-side compaction because repacking is CPU-heavy and can create availability problems.

open_codes.label: S3 distribution of compacted packs
open_codes.rationale: Replicas obtain already-compacted packfiles from S3 instead of generating them locally, shifting the scaling cost from replica CPU to network bandwidth.

open_codes.label: CPU-heavy repacking burden
open_codes.rationale: Even incremental repacking consumes substantial CPU, creating a practical scaling constraint when the operation must otherwise run on every repository replica.

open_codes.label: Maintenance-induced repository failover
open_codes.rationale: The document reports that accidentally triggering maintenance on multiple nodes for the same repository can cause the repository to fail over, making availability a key force behind primary-only compaction.

open_codes.label: Filesystem monitoring for modified-path discovery
open_codes.rationale: The repository uses Git’s fsmonitor feature to identify paths modified since the last index update, avoiding an unrestricted scan of the working directory.

open_codes.label: Watchman-based filesystem monitoring
open_codes.rationale: Scalar configures the repository to use the Watchman tool alongside Git’s fsmonitor support to discover modified paths.

open_codes.label: Selective inspection of modified paths
open_codes.rationale: After discovering changes, Git inspects only the modified paths rather than every populated path, reducing work for large working directories.

open_codes.label: Large sparse-checkout working set
open_codes.rationale: The document describes repositories with hundreds of thousands of populated files out of millions of tracked files, establishing the scale constraint that motivates optimized modified-file detection.

open_codes.label: Reduced git-status latency
open_codes.rationale: With fsmonitor enabled, git status completes in 1.5 seconds instead of 12.2 seconds for the cited large working set.

open_codes.label: Reliable Git repository hosting
open_codes.rationale: The document describes building Origin to prevent developers and CI systems from being blocked by repository push and pull failures, making hosting reliability a central architectural objective.

open_codes.label: Scalable version-control platform
open_codes.rationale: Origin is presented as a platform intended to address increasing code volume, pull requests, and CI runs while providing more scale for customers.

open_codes.label: Performance-oriented repository infrastructure
open_codes.rationale: The stated focus includes improving performance alongside reliability and scale, indicating performance as a deliberate property of the platform being built.

open_codes.label: Low-disruption migration path
open_codes.rationale: The platform is designed to provide a smooth off-ramp and make migration as painless as possible, identifying migration ease as an adopted operational and architectural concern.

open_codes.label: Evolutionary version-control architecture
open_codes.rationale: The team commits to continuing to evolve its platform as the version-control landscape changes, rather than treating the initial system as fixed.

open_codes.label: GVFS object-transfer protocol
open_codes.rationale: The teams created GVFS to reduce the amount of Git object data transferred for very large repositories, addressing the server, client, network, and object-verification costs of complete clones.

open_codes.label: Central-server coupling for missing objects
open_codes.rationale: GVFS deliberately relaxes Git’s fully distributed model by relying somewhat more on a central server to provide objects that are not present locally.

open_codes.label: Commits-and-trees-only initial clone
open_codes.rationale: The initial GVFS clone downloads pack-files containing commits and trees while omitting other objects, providing enough data for working-directory views and history inspection with substantially less transfer.

open_codes.label: On-demand Git object retrieval
open_codes.rationale: GVFS dynamically downloads missing Git objects as they are needed, avoiding transfer of the complete object history during the initial clone.

open_codes.label: Sparse-checkout and object-transfer coordination
open_codes.rationale: The document connects sparse checkout with reduced object transfer: a smaller populated working directory requires fewer objects, so the two mechanisms reinforce each other for large repositories.

open_codes.label: Co-located GVFS cache servers
open_codes.rationale: GVFS requests can be proxied through cache servers located near end users and build machines, an architectural choice intended to improve scalability of object delivery.

open_codes.label: Complete object-transfer burden
open_codes.rationale: A conventional complete copy requires transferring more than 100 GB for the Windows repository and verifying roughly 90 million objects, creating substantial network, server, client, and latency costs.

open_codes.label: Reduced transfer latency and central-server stress
open_codes.rationale: Proxy caching is reported to increase throughput and reduce latency while also decreasing load on the central server.

open_codes.label: Sparse-checkout repository design
open_codes.rationale: The document presents sparse-checkout as a repository design approach that allows developers to populate only a fraction of the repository while retaining the paths needed for daily work. It is especially relevant when repositories contain many tracked files.

open_codes.label: Sparse working directory as the default clone mode
open_codes.rationale: Scalar adopts sparse working directories by making them the default behavior of `scalar clone`, reducing client-side populated size for large repositories.

open_codes.label: Root-directory initial population
open_codes.rationale: The default sparse mode initially populates only files in the repository root, deferring additional directory population until the user requests it. This limits initial data transfer and working-directory work.

open_codes.label: Full-clone override
open_codes.rationale: The document identifies a full working-directory clone as an alternative to the sparse default and exposes it through the `--full-clone` option. The option is supported for users who need all tracked files populated.

open_codes.label: Populated-file minimization priority
open_codes.rationale: The document prioritizes minimizing the number of populated files over minimizing total repository paths because populating files involves substantially more data handling than adjusting index entries.

open_codes.label: High cost of populated-file modification detection
open_codes.rationale: Determining which populated files users modified is described as even more expensive than populating files, establishing an operational cost that strengthens the sparse-population design rationale.

open_codes.label: Three-phase commit for replica synchronization
open_codes.rationale: The document identifies three-phase commit as the core mechanism for keeping replicas synchronized and describes replicas responding to a coordinator’s prepare, commit, or rollback instructions.

open_codes.label: Git reference-update transactions
open_codes.rationale: Transactions for Git reference updates were implemented in Git and exposed through interfaces such as `git update-ref --stdin`, enabling coordinated updates across replicas.

open_codes.label: Deterministic transaction results across replicas
open_codes.rationale: The implementation includes work to ensure that reference-update transactions produce deterministic results on every replica, which is necessary for consistent replica state.

open_codes.label: Pre-transaction acquisition of local reference locks
open_codes.rationale: Git acquires all necessary local reference locks before validating or committing a reference-update transaction, coordinating concurrent access to references.

open_codes.label: Reference-value validation before commit
open_codes.rationale: Before committing, Git verifies that old reference values match expectations and that proposed new values are valid, preventing inconsistent updates.

open_codes.label: Atomic transaction rollback
open_codes.rationale: When validation fails, the entire tentative reference-update transaction is rolled back rather than partially applied, preserving consistency.

open_codes.label: Reference-operation speedups
open_codes.rationale: The teams implemented multiple performance improvements for reference-related operations to reduce the time required to update a reference on an individual replica, in addition to addressing network latency.

open_codes.label: Write-ahead log in S3 as repository source of truth
open_codes.rationale: Continuity treats local repository copies as warm caches and keeps authoritative state in an S3-backed write-ahead log, allowing repository instances to exist on any server.

open_codes.label: Stateless repository placement
open_codes.rationale: The system does not require authoritative per-repository placement state; any server can serve a repository, and missing local state can be reconstructed from the WAL.

open_codes.label: Per-server repository location tracking
open_codes.rationale: The document contrasts Continuity with Spokes by rejecting the need to track the location of every repository on every server, because such tracking makes clusters difficult to operate.

open_codes.label: On-demand repository materialization from the WAL
open_codes.rationale: When a repository is absent from a host's local disk, the system reconstructs it from the S3 WAL; avoiding constant materialization preserves efficiency while retaining flexible placement.

open_codes.label: Rendezvous-hashed repository routing
open_codes.rationale: In healthy production operation, rendezvous hashing maps repository IDs to expected nodes, using only the repository ID and the current set of healthy cluster nodes as routing state.

open_codes.label: Stale-routing tolerance
open_codes.rationale: Routing state is allowed to become inconsistent, such as after a node failure; the system prioritizes correctness under degradation by materializing the repository on a newly selected node.

open_codes.label: Consensus-free repository primaries
open_codes.rationale: Continuity avoids elections and consensus over which server is primary; any server may accept a push, which removes the operational coordination required for primary ownership.

open_codes.label: S3 atomic compare-and-swap for WAL updates
open_codes.rationale: Concurrent updates to the write-ahead log are synchronized through atomic CAS operations on S3, making it safe for any repository instance to receive a push.

open_codes.label: Block-level filesystem replication
open_codes.rationale: The teams tried replicating the filesystem at the block level to support repository distribution, but the approach was abandoned because it was operationally terrible and did not provide sufficient performance.

open_codes.label: GFS-based repository storage
open_codes.rationale: GFS was used in a short-lived deployment for distributed repository storage, but it hit the same fundamental limitations as the other networked-filesystem approaches and was not retained.

open_codes.label: DRBD-based repository storage
open_codes.rationale: DRBD supported a longer-lived attempt to replicate repository storage, but it was ultimately rejected because day-to-day operation was poor and performance gains were inadequate.

open_codes.label: Size-minimizing packfile layout
open_codes.rationale: Packfiles are generated primarily to minimize their size, resulting in objects being distributed throughout the pack rather than laid out according to their positions in the Git object graph.

open_codes.label: Delta-compressed packfile objects
open_codes.rationale: Most objects are stored as deltas on top of other objects in the same packfile rather than as complete objects, reducing storage size but requiring additional physical hops during reads.

open_codes.label: Networked filesystem for repository operations
open_codes.rationale: The document explains that Git’s random walks across large packfiles do not work effectively on file- or block-replicated networked filesystems, because acceptable performance would require caching the whole file locally, which is infeasible with hundreds of thousands of repositories.

open_codes.label: RPC access to dedicated repository fileservers
open_codes.rationale: GitHub gave up distributing the filesystem, placed repositories on dedicated fileservers, developed an RPC system, and changed the Rails application to perform repository operations remotely.

open_codes.label: Horizontal scalability without repository redundancy
open_codes.rationale: The RPC/fileserver architecture provided substantial horizontal scalability, but each repository remained on only one machine, leaving availability and performance for the busiest repositories unresolved.

open_codes.label: Chaos-monkey testing on file servers
open_codes.rationale: The team explicitly does not use random single-node failure testing on Spokes file servers because abrupt interruptions would disrupt long-running reads.

open_codes.label: Quiesced rolling reboots
open_codes.rationale: The adopted substitute for chaos testing is to quiesce and reboot servers sequentially when maintenance requires a reboot, preserving outstanding read operations while still exercising failover behavior.

open_codes.label: Rack-based availability zones
open_codes.rationale: Racks are treated as availability zones, providing the basis for organizing maintenance and failure isolation at rack granularity.

open_codes.label: Whole-rack quiescing
open_codes.rationale: The team quiesces an entire rack before proceeding with its reboots, rather than independently rebooting servers without rack-level coordination.

open_codes.label: Five-server reboot concurrency limit
open_codes.rationale: After servers finish quiescing, no more than five servers in a rack are rebooted at once, limiting the scope of simultaneous disruption while keeping rolling maintenance practical.

open_codes.label: Unplanned server unplugging for retirement
open_codes.rationale: Simply unplugging a server is rejected because it interrupts in-progress reads and temporarily reduces every hosted repository from three copies to two, increasing exposure to another failure and later write rejection.

open_codes.label: Two-copy degraded repository state
open_codes.rationale: A suddenly missing server leaves its repositories with two copies; this supports reads and writes but cannot tolerate an additional failure, creating several hours of elevated operational risk.

open_codes.label: On-disk repositories as consensus source of truth
open_codes.rationale: Spokes relies on repository copies stored on disk as the authoritative basis for consensus, making the state of every replicated copy operationally critical.

open_codes.label: Pet-style repository operations
open_codes.rationale: The document frames repositories as “pets, not cattle,” requiring individualized knowledge, monitoring, validation, and repair rather than interchangeable infrastructure treatment.

open_codes.label: Repository-to-machine routing table
open_codes.rationale: An external database is used to track exactly where every repository is replicated, providing the routing information needed to locate copies across machines.

open_codes.label: External routing-database dependency
open_codes.rationale: The routing table introduces an additional external dependency and a potential availability issue for large-scale repository operations.

open_codes.label: Continuously updated repository checksums
open_codes.rationale: Every repository is checksummed and the checksum information is continually updated in the routing table to validate on-disk copies.

open_codes.label: Automated repository repair scheduling
open_codes.rationale: When a repository copy becomes unhealthy, the system must detect the problem and schedule a repair job to restore it to a healthy state.

open_codes.label: Replica quorum for push acceptance
open_codes.rationale: The system requires sufficient healthy repository copies to maintain quorum; with two of three copies corrupt, it can no longer accept pushes.

open_codes.label: High operational burden at scale
open_codes.rationale: The combination of per-repository location tracking, continuous integrity checks, rapid failure detection, and repair makes Spokes difficult and costly to operate at scale.

open_codes.label: Compressed Git index
open_codes.rationale: Scalar registration adds compression to the .git/index file, reducing local repository metadata overhead for large repositories.

open_codes.label: Hourly background remote fetching
open_codes.rationale: Scalar configures periodic background git fetch operations to keep client repositories synchronized with their remotes without requiring users to initiate every fetch.

open_codes.label: Automatic commit-graph and multi-pack-index maintenance
open_codes.rationale: Scalar updates advanced Git data structures in the background, supporting efficient repository operations as repository history and pack data grow.

open_codes.label: Builtin file system monitor
open_codes.rationale: On macOS and Windows, Scalar configures Git's builtin file system monitor to accelerate commands such as git status and git add in large working directories.

open_codes.label: Partial clone for checkout-specific downloads
open_codes.rationale: Scalar clone uses Git's partial clone feature so a client downloads only the files needed for the current checkout, reducing initial transfer and local storage requirements.

open_codes.label: Sparse checkout working directories
open_codes.rationale: Scalar clone enables sparse-checkout to minimize the number of files materialized in the working directory, limiting client filesystem and command overhead for large repositories.

open_codes.label: Separate source and build-artifact directories
open_codes.rationale: Scalar clone places the repository inside /src so build artifacts can be stored outside the Git repository, such as in /bin or /packages, avoiding unnecessary repository working-tree contents.

open_codes.label: Virtualized filesystem for repository-scale access
open_codes.rationale: VFS for Git uses a virtualized filesystem to bypass assumptions about repository size and enable the Windows repository to operate at previously impractical scale. This approach addresses the storage and performance costs of Git repositories containing complete history.

open_codes.label: Native Git scalability improvements without filesystem virtualization
open_codes.rationale: Microsoft began a separate effort to support very large repositories without requiring a virtualized filesystem, shifting scalability work into Git itself so the improvements could benefit repositories and users more broadly.

open_codes.label: Commit-graph file
open_codes.rationale: The commit-graph file is identified as a contribution to the Git client intended to improve performance for large repositories, particularly by reducing the cost of history-related operations.

open_codes.label: Sparse-checkout performance improvements
open_codes.rationale: Improvements to sparse-checkout are listed among the Git client changes developed to reduce the amount of repository data that must be handled locally, supporting large-repository workflows.

open_codes.label: Recommended Git configuration values
open_codes.rationale: Scalar accelerates Git commands by setting configuration values recommended for repository-scale performance rather than requiring users to tune Git manually.

open_codes.label: Background repository maintenance
open_codes.rationale: Scalar runs maintenance in the background to improve Git command performance while reducing the need for developers to wait for maintenance work during interactive operations.

open_codes.label: GVFS-protocol cloning through Azure Repos
open_codes.rationale: Scalar supports cloning through the GVFS protocol when the repository is hosted by Azure Repos, providing a protocol-specific scaling path for extremely large repositories such as Microsoft Office.

open_codes.label: Repository performance tracing and user-feedback analysis
open_codes.rationale: Microsoft used a custom tracing system and user feedback to identify performance bottlenecks, providing the diagnostic basis for prioritizing client and repository-scale improvements.

open_codes.label: Rails monolith architecture
open_codes.rationale: GitHub’s platform started as and mostly remained a Rails monolith, establishing the application architecture whose scaling constraints shaped repository-storage decisions.

open_codes.label: Co-located repository copies on local disk
open_codes.rationale: The initial deployment placed repository copies on disk next to the Ruby server, using local filesystem access before horizontal scaling created a shared-storage problem.

open_codes.label: Horizontal scaling through additional Rails instances
open_codes.rationale: The article presents deploying more application instances as the normal way to scale Rails; with Git repositories, this creates the requirement for every instance to access repository data.

open_codes.label: Filesystem-level distribution of Git data
open_codes.rationale: The early systems team chose to distribute the filesystem rather than change Git or operate directly on packfiles, intending to preserve the Rails application and avoid Git-specific implementation work.

open_codes.label: Centralized NFS repository storage
open_codes.rationale: NFS was considered as the most obvious centralized distributed-filesystem design for all repositories, but the team explicitly discarded it because Git’s filesystem assumptions did not work reliably over the network.

open_codes.label: Local-filesystem semantics for Git operations
open_codes.rationale: Git’s default behavior assumes local filesystem properties such as locking, tearing, reading, and syncing; these assumptions are a key compatibility constraint when selecting repository-storage architecture.

open_codes.label: Network-filesystem performance and correctness problems
open_codes.rationale: The attempted networked-filesystem approaches produced slow and buggy behavior, demonstrating the operational and quality trade-offs that prevented filesystem distribution from solving the scaling problem.

open_codes.label: Custom Git client dependency
open_codes.rationale: Scalar currently requires a custom Git version, demonstrated by the documented version requirement. This is a client-side architectural constraint for accelerating very large repositories.

open_codes.label: Core Git feature contribution plan
open_codes.rationale: The team plans to contribute Scalar’s features to the core Git client so that the custom Git requirement can eventually be removed.

open_codes.label: Repository registration as activation mechanism
open_codes.rationale: Users must run `scalar register` from a repository to make Scalar aware of it and activate Scalar-specific local configuration and maintenance.

open_codes.label: Background repository maintenance
open_codes.rationale: Registering a repository starts background maintenance intended to accelerate Git commands in existing, potentially very large repositories.

open_codes.label: Maintenance pause and unregister controls
open_codes.rationale: Scalar provides `scalar pause` to delay maintenance and `scalar unregister` to stop future maintenance, making background activity controllable by repository users.

open_codes.label: Commit-graph generation and verification
open_codes.rationale: The documented maintenance log shows Scalar writing a Git commit graph and then verifying it, using commit-graph structures to support repository-scale performance.

open_codes.label: Background repository maintenance
open_codes.rationale: VFS for Git and Scalar maintain repositories through background processes so users do not wait for expensive maintenance operations during commands such as commit or fetch.

open_codes.label: Incremental maintenance operations
open_codes.rationale: The document states that VFS for Git and Scalar perform background maintenance incrementally to reduce the additional CPU and memory load on the client machine.

open_codes.label: Foreground automatic garbage collection
open_codes.rationale: The conventional Git approach runs automatic garbage collection at the end of common commands, but the lesson rejects making users wait for this expensive foreground operation because it can block commands for minutes.

open_codes.label: Disabling automatic garbage collection
open_codes.rationale: Setting gc.auto to zero is presented as an available alternative, but it is not the adopted solution because accumulated objects cause repository performance to decay over time.

open_codes.label: Command blocking from garbage collection
open_codes.rationale: Automatic garbage collection can block simple operations such as git commit for minutes when it performs a complete object-data rewrite and compression step.

open_codes.label: System-wide resource exhaustion during repository rewrites
open_codes.rationale: Rewriting tens of gigabytes can consume all available CPU and memory, bringing the entire system to a standstill.

open_codes.label: Repository performance decay after GC disabling
open_codes.rationale: When automatic garbage collection is disabled, new objects accumulate through daily work and repository performance gradually deteriorates.

open_codes.label: Automatic garbage-collection suppression
open_codes.rationale: Scalar sets `gc.auto=0` so ordinary Git commands are not blocked by expensive maintenance; repository cleanup is delegated to background maintenance.

open_codes.label: Background Git object-database maintenance
open_codes.rationale: Background maintenance keeps the Git object database clean while avoiding maintenance work during interactive Git commands.

open_codes.label: Fetch-time commit-graph writing suppression
open_codes.rationale: Scalar sets `fetch.writeCommitGraph=false` to prevent `git fetch` from performing commit-graph writes synchronously.

open_codes.label: Background commit-graph generation
open_codes.rationale: Commit graphs are written in the background rather than during fetch, reducing the interactive cost of repository synchronization.

open_codes.label: Ahead-behind status calculation suppression
open_codes.rationale: Scalar sets `status.aheadBehind=false` to remove the potentially expensive calculation comparing the local branch with its remote-tracking branch.

open_codes.label: Watchman-backed filesystem monitoring hook
open_codes.rationale: Scalar configures `core.fsmonitor` to use a hook communicating with Watchman when Watchman is installed, supporting faster detection of working-tree changes.

open_codes.label: Background configuration refresh for registered repositories
open_codes.rationale: The configuration step runs in the background so newer Scalar versions can update settings in registered repositories after installation.

open_codes.label: S3-backed write-ahead log
open_codes.rationale: The system stores the write-ahead log in S3, using S3 as the durable, highly scalable source of truth from which replicas can catch up.

open_codes.label: Optimistic UDP gossip replication
open_codes.rationale: Replicas disseminate catch-up metadata through gossip UDP packets rather than relying on reliable transport; lost or misrouted packets are tolerated because reads verify state against S3.

open_codes.label: Direct replica catch-up from S3
open_codes.rationale: Each replica uses the metadata received through gossip to retrieve the required WAL state directly from S3, avoiding dependence on another replica for synchronization.

open_codes.label: ETag-conditional read verification
open_codes.rationale: Before serving a fetch or clone, a replica performs a conditional S3 GET using the ETag of the WAL index it has processed; a current ETag confirms freshness, while a changed ETag triggers catch-up.

open_codes.label: Globally consistent replica reads
open_codes.rationale: The S3 verification mechanism makes reads from all replicas fully consistent, including when replication packets are lost or network topology changes.

open_codes.label: Elastic per-repository replica sizing
open_codes.rationale: The architecture assigns replicas according to repository demand: large monorepositories can use hundreds of replicas for CI load, while tiny repositories can use one replica because S3 provides the authoritative copy.

open_codes.label: Idle-replica disk garbage collection
open_codes.rationale: Replicas that have received no traffic for a while are removed from node disk and materialized again from the WAL when a subsequent fetch arrives, reducing storage use for inactive repositories.

open_codes.label: Sparse-checkout scalar clone
open_codes.rationale: The clone uses Git sparse-checkout so the initial working directory contains only a limited subset of repository files, reducing client-side work for a large repository.

open_codes.label: Cone-mode sparse-checkout
open_codes.rationale: The sparse-checkout configuration uses cone mode, restricting the initial working tree to root-level files and supporting scalable selection of repository content.

open_codes.label: Incremental working-tree expansion
open_codes.rationale: Additional files are made available with `git sparse-checkout set`, allowing clients to expand the working directory only when needed instead of materializing the entire repository immediately.

open_codes.label: Full working-tree materialization option
open_codes.rationale: The document provides `git sparse-checkout disable` as the mechanism for fully populating the working directory when a complete checkout is required.

open_codes.label: Nested source working directory
open_codes.rationale: The clone places the repository under a `scalar` directory with the working directory inside a nested `src` directory, creating room for sibling directories outside the source tree.

open_codes.label: Sibling build-output directories
open_codes.rationale: The nested source layout enables build output files to reside in sibling directories, preventing Git from having to manage those files in the repository working directory.

open_codes.label: Reduced Git work-tree management load
open_codes.rationale: The described sparse checkout and directory layout reduce the work Git performs while managing the repository, which the document identifies as a lesson for improving Git speed.

open_codes.label: Incremental pack-file repacking
open_codes.rationale: Scalar adopts incremental repacking instead of rewriting the entire repository at once, selecting batches of small pack-files to control pack-file growth and maintenance impact.

open_codes.label: Multi-pack-index-based repack coordination
open_codes.rationale: The multi-pack-index is used to identify the objects being repacked and to coordinate the transition from old pack-files to the newly created pack-file.

open_codes.label: Object-reference redirection to new pack-files
open_codes.rationale: After adding a new pack-file, Git updates multi-pack-index object references so processes using the new index read from the new pack-file rather than the old ones.

open_codes.label: Deferred obsolete-pack deletion
open_codes.rationale: Old pack-files are retained until the multi-pack-index shows that they have no referenced objects, preventing deletion while they may still be needed.

open_codes.label: Two-step repack-and-expire maintenance
open_codes.rationale: The system separates `git multi-pack-index repack` from `git multi-pack-index expire` to avoid disrupting foreground Git commands run by users.

open_codes.label: Pack-file count and storage reduction
open_codes.rationale: Deployment results show repositories improving from thousands of packs totaling 150–200 GB to fewer than one hundred packs totaling 30–50 GB, demonstrating reduced storage costs and pack-management pressure.

open_codes.label: File-handle scalability pressure
open_codes.rationale: Unbounded pack-file growth creates a client-side scalability problem because Git cannot keep file handles open for all pack-files simultaneously.

open_codes.label: WAL-first storage architecture
open_codes.rationale: Continuity uses a write-ahead-log-first design to provide consistent horizontal scaling while preserving hard durability and consistency guarantees.

open_codes.label: Fully consistent replica cluster
open_codes.rationale: All replicas are described as fully consistent, enabling the same repository state to serve Git protocol operations and Origin RPC operations across nodes.

open_codes.label: Arbitrary replica horizontal scaling
open_codes.rationale: The architecture permits deployment of an arbitrary number of replicas, with read-only Git-operation throughput growing linearly as replicas are added.

open_codes.label: Replicated WAL updates on object storage
open_codes.rationale: Cluster push throughput is governed by the latency of updating the WAL on S3, while compacted data is replicated to the other nodes.

open_codes.label: S3 Standard storage tier
open_codes.rationale: S3 Standard is used for clusters that sustain push ingestion while compacting and replicating data, providing a stated throughput level of up to 120 pushes per second.

open_codes.label: S3 Express One Zone storage tier
open_codes.rationale: High-performance clusters are deployed on S3 Express One Zone to obtain lower PUT latency and higher push-ingestion throughput than S3 Standard.

open_codes.label: Replication-compaction coupling
open_codes.rationale: The document identifies replication and compaction as interdependent scaling factors: replicated pushes require compaction to be replicated or performed independently on each replica, and increased push rates degrade read performance through compaction work.

open_codes.label: Git compaction throughput bottleneck
open_codes.rationale: With lower-latency S3 Express One Zone, object-storage latency is no longer the limiting factor; the system is effectively constrained by Git's ability to compact on-disk data.

open_codes.label: Git-integrated custom filesystem watcher
open_codes.rationale: Scalar uses a custom watcher in Git rather than the more general Watchman so the watcher can understand Git semantics such as .gitignore patterns and avoid unnecessary scans. This supports scaling repositories with growing modified size.

open_codes.label: Sparse-checkout for populated-size scaling
open_codes.rationale: The document identifies sparse-checkout as the adopted mechanism for scaling repository populated size by avoiding a complete working-tree population, while noting that the feature still requires further improvement.

open_codes.label: Virtualized filesystem for populated-size scaling
open_codes.rationale: VFS for Git is no longer the approach used by Scalar; the document contrasts its virtualization and deferred-cost behavior with the current sparse-checkout approach.

open_codes.label: Parallel checkout processing
open_codes.rationale: The document identifies checkout as a new bottleneck after moving away from virtualization and reports investigation of a parallel implementation to improve performance. The resulting performance effect is not yet reported as an achieved outcome.

open_codes.label: Partial-clone interface for GVFS protocol integration
open_codes.rationale: Scalar reworked Git's interaction with the GVFS protocol so that it operates through Git's partial-clone interface, allowing improvements to the two experiences to benefit each other and avoiding local copies of every reachable object.

open_codes.label: GVFS-style object-download cache servers
open_codes.rationale: The document proposes separating branch-update authority from pack-file delivery through an additional fetch-objects endpoint, reflecting the need to serve many engineers and build machines without making the central server handle every object transfer.

open_codes.label: Periodic foreground garbage collection for very large repositories
open_codes.rationale: The document states that relying on periodic foreground garbage collection is not feasible for very large repositories, motivating a planned shift toward background maintenance in the core Git client.

open_codes.label: Checkout performance regression after virtualization removal
open_codes.rationale: The document reports that git checkout is slower with sparse-checkout than it was with VFS for Git because virtualization could defer populated-size costs; this is an observed performance trade-off rather than a newly adopted design.

open_codes.label: Reduced Scalar scope
open_codes.rationale: The document explicitly states that Scalar is intentionally being made to do less, limiting its role as Git itself gains needed capabilities.

open_codes.label: Core Git capability investment
open_codes.rationale: The team is investing in making core Git do more, including planned contributions that address capabilities currently supplied by Scalar.

open_codes.label: Scalar as an interim performance layer
open_codes.rationale: Scalar is described as the mechanism used to obtain the performance required today while Git’s native capabilities improve.

open_codes.label: Transition to core Git without Scalar
open_codes.rationale: The intended direction is to move from using Scalar to relying only on the core Git client as Git improves.

open_codes.label: Persistent Scalar dependency
open_codes.rationale: The document frames continued reliance on Scalar as something the planned Git improvements are intended to eliminate, rather than the desired long-term architecture.

open_codes.label: Removal of management layers above Git
open_codes.rationale: Scalar serves as an example of features that should be incorporated into Git so that additional management layers are no longer needed.

open_codes.label: Distributed version control for decentralized kernel development
open_codes.rationale: Git was designed as a distributed replacement for BitKeeper because Linux kernel development involved many maintainers working across decentralized subsystems. The distributed architecture fit that workflow.

open_codes.label: Centralized repository hosting for organizational workflows
open_codes.rationale: Although users retain distributed-model capabilities, the document describes open-source projects and companies as relying heavily on a centralized host rather than operating through a fully decentralized workflow.

open_codes.label: Offline work capability
open_codes.rationale: The document identifies working offline as a retained advantage of Git's distributed model, relevant to client-side repository architecture.

open_codes.label: Delayed push capability
open_codes.rationale: The document identifies delaying pushes as another distributed-model advantage retained by users even when they rely on centralized hosting.

open_codes.label: Git hosting scalability difficulty
open_codes.rationale: The document characterizes hosting Git repositories at scale as exceptionally difficult, establishing repository scale as a major architectural and operational challenge.

open_codes.label: Distributed-model and centralized-workflow mismatch
open_codes.rationale: The document reports that Git's distributed nature can hinder typical projects and companies because their workflows are not decentralized, despite their use of selected distributed capabilities.

open_codes.label: Loose-object cleanup
open_codes.rationale: The maintenance step removes accumulated loose-object overhead, addressing the performance and disk-space costs of storing objects individually.

open_codes.label: Pack-file delta compression
open_codes.rationale: Pack-files are used because delta encoding stores Git objects more compactly than separate loose-object files, reducing storage overhead at scale.

open_codes.label: Single-pack repacking
open_codes.rationale: Consolidating accumulated pack-files into one pack-file is described as the normal garbage-collection approach, but rewriting all data becomes impractical when the repository contains too much data.

open_codes.label: Multi-pack index
open_codes.rationale: The document identifies the Git multi-pack-index as the adopted solution for maintaining efficient object lookup across multiple pack-files without rewriting all repository data into one pack-file.

open_codes.label: Cross-pack object-location tracking
open_codes.rationale: The multi-pack index records where objects reside across multiple pack-files, preserving lookup performance while enabling smaller maintenance steps.

open_codes.label: Background multi-pack-index generation
open_codes.rationale: Scalar runs the multi-pack-index write operation in the background, making index creation a background maintenance activity rather than an operation that blocks foreground work.

open_codes.label: Pack-index scan growth
open_codes.rationale: As pack-files accumulate, inspecting a long list of individual pack-indexes makes object lookup slower; this is the performance problem the multi-pack index addresses.

open_codes.label: Loose-object storage overhead
open_codes.rationale: Accumulating loose objects is reported to consume more disk space and create significant performance drawbacks compared with packed storage.

open_codes.label: DRBD filesystem block-level replication
open_codes.rationale: The earlier repository-replication architecture was abandoned because its sensitivity to latency required replicas to remain colocated, which was considered undesirable and motivated development of Spokes.

open_codes.label: Spokes repository replication
open_codes.rationale: Spokes was adopted to replace DRBD and enable repository replicas to be placed farther apart, supporting distant-replica operation for a very large repository population.

open_codes.label: Distant Spokes replica placement
open_codes.rationale: The engineering team runs Spokes replicas at increasing distances and treats geographic separation as an important scalability capability, despite the resulting inter-replica latency.

open_codes.label: Inter-replica latency as reference-update throughput constraint
open_codes.rationale: Greater replica distance increases synchronization latency and reduces the maximum reference-update rate sustainable per repository; this is especially consequential for repositories with unusually frequent user or internally generated reference updates.

open_codes.label: Reference-update amplification from pull-request bookkeeping
open_codes.rationale: A single user push can produce many additional reference updates, including synchronization, test-merge, and test-rebase references; in some repositories one push triggers more than one hundred updates, increasing the write scalability burden on replicated repositories.

open_codes.label: Per-repository reference-update latency budget
open_codes.rationale: Spokes must support at least a few reference updates per second in one repository, implying a budget of a few hundred milliseconds per update; this requirement is driven by high-latency replicas and unexpected high-activity workflows.

open_codes.label: Read-preserving write optimization
open_codes.rationale: Any mechanism used to accelerate replicated reference writes must avoid degrading reads, because repository reads outnumber writes by approximately 100 to 1.

open_codes.label: Identical distributed repository instances
open_codes.rationale: Git's distributed version-control model makes every repository instance identical, so a hosted repository has no inherently special server-side representation. This creates the architectural constraint that server-side scaling must preserve repository equivalence.

open_codes.label: Packfile-based repository storage
open_codes.rationale: Git compresses code and metadata into packfiles for repository storage. The document presents packfiles as a fundamental part of Git's storage design and therefore as the existing storage choice that hosting systems must accommodate.

open_codes.label: Packfile-based Git networking
open_codes.rationale: Push and fetch operations transfer packfiles, and the server is required to receive and send them over the network. This constrains server-side alternatives because client-facing Git operations must remain packfile-compatible.

open_codes.label: Filesystem-resident packfiles
open_codes.rationale: Packfiles must exist on a filesystem for Git to access them. This implementation constraint makes packfile storage difficult to distribute across many disks and machines.

open_codes.label: HTTP front end over a single on-disk repository
open_codes.rationale: The document presents placing an HTTP daemon in front of one on-disk repository as the simple hosting approach, but explains that it has a very low scalability and reliability ceiling; it is therefore not suitable for repositories hosted at scale.

open_codes.label: Packfile-induced availability limitation
open_codes.rationale: Companies hosting Git at scale found that the packfile-based design limited availability because large packfiles had to reside on filesystem-backed storage, making repository access vulnerable to server or storage failures.

open_codes.label: Packfile-induced scalability limitation
open_codes.rationale: The document reports that packfiles limited scalability: large binary files are difficult to manage across many servers, while the simple single-machine design cannot support sufficiently parallel Git operations.

open_codes.label: Multi-disk and multi-machine repository placement
open_codes.rationale: The document identifies distributing a repository across many disks and machines as the desired direction for parallel Git operations and continued availability after server crashes, while leaving the implementation challenge unresolved.

open_codes.label: Three-phase commit consensus
open_codes.rationale: Spokes uses three-phase commit because it maps elegantly to the Git transaction model and provides fully consistent repository operations across replicas.

open_codes.label: Three-replica repository replication
open_codes.rationale: The system initially adopted three replicas per repository as the capacity and redundancy sweet spot, allowing continued push acceptance after one machine failure.

open_codes.label: Fixed replication floor for small repositories
open_codes.rationale: Spokes retains three replicas even for vast numbers of small or throwaway repositories because reducing the replica count would compromise full consistency and create data-loss risk.

open_codes.label: Consensus latency bound by the slowest replica
open_codes.rationale: Every three-phase-commit step is constrained by the slowest server in the cluster, making replica latency a central scalability force.

open_codes.label: Horizontal scalability ceiling for large repositories
open_codes.rationale: Three replicas cannot provide sufficient traffic capacity for massive enterprise monorepos, especially under CI load; adding replicas is limited by the resulting tail-at-scale effects.

open_codes.label: Push-throughput degradation with replica count
open_codes.rationale: The document reports that increasing the number of replicas worsens push throughput because each consensus step waits on the slowest participant.

open_codes.label: Idle-replica resource overhead
open_codes.rationale: The three-replica minimum forces Spokes to maintain mostly idle copies for numerous small, barely used repositories, producing a high resource floor at large repository counts.

open_codes.label: Primary heartbeat failure detection
open_codes.rationale: The document explicitly states that Spokes uses heartbeats, but not as its primary mechanism for detecting failed nodes.

open_codes.label: Heartbeat-based load polling and recovery confirmation
open_codes.rationale: Heartbeats are adopted for polling system load and for providing an all-clear signal that marks a previously offline node online again.

open_codes.label: Preference-ordered replica lists
open_codes.rationale: Routing queries return several up-to-date repository replicas in preference order, allowing operations to select the preferred available copy.

open_codes.label: Operation-level replica failover
open_codes.rationale: For clean failures such as refused connections or timeouts, each operation tries another repository replica when the first-choice host fails.

open_codes.label: Advisory node-offline detection
open_codes.rationale: Offline detection is used only as an optimization: it changes routing preference temporarily rather than serving as an authoritative determination that a node cannot be used.

open_codes.label: Replica retention after repeated failures
open_codes.rationale: After three consecutive failures, a replica is moved to the end of the read preference order instead of being removed, preserving the possibility of using it if other replicas fail.

open_codes.label: RPC failover pattern monitoring
open_codes.rationale: The team uses graphs of RPCs redirected between servers as its best detector for discovering misbehaving or unavailable servers, complementing per-operation failure handling.

open_codes.label: Per-application-server failure views
open_codes.rationale: Failure detection is deliberately MxN: each application server maintains its own list of file servers considered offline, limiting the impact of network-local and application-server-specific faults.

open_codes.label: Git application-level replication
open_codes.rationale: Spokes performs replication at the Git application level, replacing filesystem block-level replication so repository updates can be replicated with Git-specific semantics.

open_codes.label: Filesystem block-level replication
open_codes.rationale: The older replication approach operated at the filesystem block level and was replaced by Spokes’ Git application-level approach.

open_codes.label: Proxy-mediated multi-fileserver replication
open_codes.rationale: Every repository push passes through a proxy that transparently replicates the update to multiple fileservers, separating client-facing pushes from replica distribution.

open_codes.label: Quorum-based update durability
open_codes.rationale: Spokes is designed to replicate every Git update safely to all replicas in most cases and to at least a quorum in every case, providing a minimum durability guarantee during failures.

open_codes.label: Geographically distributed repository replicas
open_codes.rationale: The system allows replicas to span widely separated datacenters and continents rather than keeping all copies geographically close, improving disaster survivability and enabling regional read locality.

open_codes.label: Low-latency replica proximity requirement
open_codes.rationale: Early Spokes versions required low-latency communication between the proxy and every replica to sustain high update rates, constraining replicas to nearby locations; this constraint was overcome for wider distribution.

open_codes.label: Regional read routing
open_codes.rationale: Placing replicas in multiple regions enables Git read requests to be directed to a nearby replica, reducing network transit time for users.

open_codes.label: Coalesced bookkeeping-update transactions
open_codes.rationale: Bookkeeping reference updates are combined into fewer transactions to reduce the processing burden caused by cascades of updates.

open_codes.label: Priority scheduling for user-initiated reference updates
open_codes.rationale: User-initiated updates are given priority over non-time-critical bookkeeping updates so that long bookkeeping cascades do not block or time out user requests.

open_codes.label: Closest synchronized-replica read routing
open_codes.rationale: Git fetches and clones are routed to the geographically closest Spokes replica that is sufficiently up to date, improving transfer locality while preserving read correctness.

open_codes.label: Geo-replicated Spokes replicas
open_codes.rationale: Spokes is used to replicate Git repositories across geographical locations for both GitHub.com and GitHub Enterprise, enabling users near a replica to obtain faster Git transfers.

open_codes.label: Non-voting geo-replication hosts
open_codes.rationale: Geo-replicated hosts are configured as non-voting so that pushes to the main hosts continue to work when a replica is temporarily unreachable.

open_codes.label: Replica freshness detection
open_codes.rationale: Spokes determines which replicas are up to date before routing reads, providing the mechanism needed to safely use geographically distributed replicas.

open_codes.label: Checksum-based replica state comparison
open_codes.rationale: The system uses a Spokes checksum to summarize each replica and compare whether replicas hold the same logical contents.

open_codes.label: Reference-state checksum composition
open_codes.rationale: The checksum incorporates every reference name and value, along with additional replica state, so it represents the replica’s logical contents.

open_codes.label: Per-update replica consistency checking
open_codes.rationale: A Spokes checksum is computed for every replica after each update as an additional check that replicas remain synchronized.

open_codes.label: Incremental checksum maintenance
open_codes.rationale: The checksum is updated incrementally whenever possible to avoid the expense of recomputing it from scratch in repositories with many references.

open_codes.label: Exclusive-or checksum aggregation
open_codes.rationale: The checksum is defined as the exclusive-or of the hashes of individual reference-name and value pairs, enabling efficient incremental updates.

open_codes.label: Full checksum recomputation
open_codes.rationale: Computing the checksum from scratch for every update is explicitly avoided because its cost would limit the maximum rate of reference updates.

open_codes.label: Constant-time reference-update checksum formula
open_codes.rationale: When a reference changes, the system derives the new checksum by XORing out the old pair hash and XORing in the new pair hash, using the prior checksum rather than scanning all references.

open_codes.label: Checksum equality as logical-content equivalence
open_codes.rationale: The document reports that equal Spokes checksums guarantee that two replicas contain the same logical contents.

open_codes.label: Multi-copy repository replication
open_codes.rationale: Spokes maintains at least three copies of every repository and gist to support durable, highly available access when servers or networks fail.

open_codes.label: Application-level Git replication system
open_codes.rationale: The document describes Spokes as an application-level replication system for Git, positioning replication above the underlying Git storage system.

open_codes.label: Git-and-rsync replication mechanism
open_codes.rationale: Spokes combines Git and rsync to replicate repository content, rather than relying on only one replication mechanism.

open_codes.label: Repository repair and rebalancing operations
open_codes.rationale: The replication system includes repair and rebalancing as explicit operational mechanisms for maintaining replicated repositories across file servers.

open_codes.label: Working-directory inspection by core commands
open_codes.rationale: The core commands—status, add, and checkout—inspect the working directory to compare Git’s view with on-disk state, making this inspection a central client-side operation that must scale with repository size.

open_codes.label: Complete tracked-path index
open_codes.rationale: The Git index represents every tracked path at the current HEAD and is read and written by each core command, providing the baseline structure for repository state inspection.

open_codes.label: Updated index file format
open_codes.rationale: The Windows OS repository uses an updated index format to reduce the size and I/O burden of an index containing millions of entries.

open_codes.label: Untracked cache
open_codes.rationale: The document recommends enabling Git’s untracked cache through the many-files feature to reduce work associated with examining large repositories.

open_codes.label: Single-file index stream I/O
open_codes.rationale: Index data is read and written as a stream from a single file, an implementation approach whose cost is primarily tied to file I/O rather than high per-entry processing overhead.

open_codes.label: Multi-million-entry index
open_codes.rationale: The Windows OS repository’s index contains more than three million entries, documenting the scale that the index-based design must support.

open_codes.label: Index compression from 400 MB to 250 MB
open_codes.rationale: The updated index format reduces the index file from 400 MB to 250 MB, lowering the amount of data that core commands must read and write.

open_codes.label: Low average index-entry processing time
open_codes.rationale: Despite the large index, the document reports that the average time per index entry is very low because the dominant cost is streaming the single index file.

open_codes.label: Three-replica repository placement
open_codes.rationale: Spokes keeps at least three replicas of every repository to preserve availability and durability through server failures.

open_codes.label: Majority write quorum with a two-replica minimum
open_codes.rationale: Writes are accepted only when a majority of replicas, and always at least two, commit the write and produce the same repository state, enforcing consistent ordering and durable storage across failures.

open_codes.label: Live-traffic-based failure detection
open_codes.rationale: Spokes determines that a server is offline by monitoring live application traffic, allowing the system to identify failures without relying on a separately described probe mechanism.

open_codes.label: Failure-aware request routing
open_codes.rationale: After detecting an offline server, Spokes routes around it so repository operations can continue despite the failure.

open_codes.label: Automated permanent-failure repair
open_codes.rationale: Spokes automatically repairs repository replication after a disk or server fails permanently, enabling rapid recovery of the desired replica level.

open_codes.label: Retirement through active-replica exclusion
open_codes.rationale: A server prepared for retirement is removed from the count of active replicas while remaining available for reads and writes; replication checks then create replacement replicas as though the server had disappeared.

open_codes.label: Rack-level availability zones
open_codes.rationale: Repository replicas are placed so that no two replicas share a rack, protecting availability and durability against rack-wide power or networking failures.

open_codes.label: Majority-based write quorum
open_codes.rationale: Spokes treats a write as durable when a majority of replicas accepts it; two of three replicas suffice, while three of four or five are required. This provides durability and continued operation despite replica failures.

open_codes.label: Per-write voting without a primary replica
open_codes.rationale: Instead of electing a primary server whose write order governs all replicas, Spokes treats every write as an election that directly selects the winning order and outcome.

open_codes.label: Rollback of non-majority writes
open_codes.rationale: Writes that cannot be applied identically at a majority are reverted on replicas where they were applied, preserving agreement among the surviving replicas.

open_codes.label: Isolation of losing replicas
open_codes.rationale: Replicas on the losing side of a write vote are marked unhealthy and removed from read and write service until repaired, preventing inconsistent replicas from serving repository traffic.

open_codes.label: Automatic replica repair
open_codes.rationale: Unhealthy replicas are repaired automatically and quickly, allowing the remaining majority to continue accepting reads and writes while recovery occurs.

open_codes.label: Periodic replica-count reconciliation
open_codes.rationale: Spokes periodically checks whether every repository has its desired number of replicas and creates additional replicas when the count is too low, including after an entire server is removed.

open_codes.label: N-to-N replica reconstruction
open_codes.rationale: After a server failure, new replicas may be created anywhere and copied from either surviving copy of each repository; recovery therefore distributes reconstruction across the cluster rather than relying on a single source or destination.

open_codes.label: Short-lived non-unanimous voting impact
open_codes.rationale: Non-unanimous votes occur only a few dozen times on a typical day, usually because a busy or timed-out replica is bypassed; the lagging replica generally recovers within minutes without visible repository-availability impact.

open_codes.label: Hourly background repository fetch
open_codes.rationale: The client runs `git fetch` approximately once per hour in the background so downloading newly received objects occurs outside the user's foreground command, keeping the local object database close to the remotes.

open_codes.label: Preservation of local and remote-tracking branches
open_codes.rationale: The background fetch intentionally leaves local branches, including `refs/remotes`, unchanged, preserving the user's normal ref-update workflow and requiring a foreground fetch when current remote refs are needed.

open_codes.label: Hidden remote-ref namespace
open_codes.rationale: A custom refspec places fetched remote refs under `refs/scalar/hidden/<remote>/<branch>`, providing starting points for commit-graph generation without changing the visible local branch and remote-tracking references.

open_codes.label: Background commit-graph maintenance
open_codes.rationale: The commit-graph is updated asynchronously rather than relying on foreground fetches, maintaining performance for repositories with hundreds of thousands of commits while avoiding additional foreground-fetch work.

open_codes.label: Reachability-based commit-graph coverage
open_codes.rationale: The background operation uses `--reachable` so the commit-graph includes every reachable commit, including commits reachable through the hidden Scalar refs.

open_codes.label: Incremental split commit-graph format
open_codes.rationale: The operation uses `--split` to update the commit-graph incrementally, minimizing the cost of repeated background maintenance on large repositories.

open_codes.label: Foreground-fetch overhead
open_codes.rationale: Writing the commit-graph during a normal foreground `git fetch` introduces extra overhead; moving that work to the background recovers time from the user-facing fetch operation.

open_codes.label: Automatic configuration of advanced Git settings
open_codes.rationale: Scalar automatically configures Git repositories to use performance features that are difficult for users to discover and tune manually, particularly for very large repositories.

open_codes.label: Core Git implementation of performance features
open_codes.rationale: The team implements new capabilities in Git rather than adding equivalent functionality to Scalar, making the underlying client more powerful while keeping Scalar small.

open_codes.label: Background maintenance in Git
open_codes.rationale: Background maintenance was ported into Git as an example of moving performance functionality into the core client, reducing Scalar-specific complexity.

open_codes.label: Scalar as a thin configuration layer
open_codes.rationale: Scalar is intentionally designed to do little more than the standard Git client, with its main role being configuration of advanced Git settings rather than duplicating Git behavior.

open_codes.label: GVFS Protocol integration
open_codes.rationale: Scalar uses the GVFS Protocol to support performance improvements associated with large repositories, although this protocol is treated as specific to Scalar and its hosting context.

open_codes.label: GVFS Protocol in the standard Git client
open_codes.rationale: The team explicitly does not intend to bring Scalar's GVFS Protocol support into standard Git; partial clone is the standardized alternative adopted by the Git project and supported by services such as GitHub.

open_codes.label: Partial clone for large-repository transfer optimization
open_codes.rationale: The document recommends partial clone when supported by the hosting service because it greatly reduces clone and fetch times and lowers the required local disk space.

open_codes.label: Default-off advanced Git features
open_codes.rationale: Advanced performance features are disabled by default for compatibility reasons, creating a trade-off between broad compatibility and out-of-the-box performance optimization.

open_codes.label: Background maintenance scheduling
open_codes.rationale: The document describes `scalar register` as providing a background maintenance schedule for repository tasks such as fetching, commit-graph updates, and object cleanup, reducing the need for users to run these operations manually.

open_codes.label: Consolidated maintenance command
open_codes.rationale: Scalar provides `scalar run all` to execute all maintenance steps in one foreground command, allowing users to run maintenance on their own schedule or alongside background maintenance.

open_codes.label: Automatic repository registration after Scalar cloning
open_codes.rationale: `scalar clone` automatically registers the new enlistment so it receives the recommended configuration and ongoing maintenance, an important mechanism for consistently managing client repositories.

open_codes.label: GVFS protocol for large repositories and user groups
open_codes.rationale: The document presents the GVFS protocol as an option for sufficiently large repositories used by large groups of users, supporting scalable repository access through Scalar cloning.

open_codes.label: Co-located GVFS cache server
open_codes.rationale: For sufficiently large repositories with many users, the document recommends setting up a cache server near the repository to handle GVFS protocol requests and provide the infrastructure needed for scalable access.

open_codes.label: GVFS deployment without cache infrastructure
open_codes.rationale: The document indicates that using the GVFS protocol without the resources to establish the required cache-server infrastructure may not be a suitable approach.

open_codes.label: Git protocol for infrastructure-constrained repositories
open_codes.rationale: When an organization cannot provide GVFS cache-server infrastructure, the document suggests using `scalar register` with an existing Git-protocol repository instead, trading the GVFS deployment requirements for the conventional protocol.

open_codes.label: Repository-size limitation of the example deployment
open_codes.rationale: The example Scalar repository is explicitly described as too small to require GVFS, illustrating that the protocol and cache-server architecture are driven by repository size and the number of users rather than being universally necessary.

open_codes.label: Consistency and partition tolerance priority
open_codes.rationale: Spokes explicitly prioritizes consistency and partition tolerance over availability, establishing the system’s resilience trade-off under node failures or communication partitions.

open_codes.label: Synchronous commitment to two replicas
open_codes.rationale: Spokes accepts a write only when it can commit the write synchronously to at least two replicas, using replica count and synchronous persistence to protect against permanent data loss.

open_codes.label: Write acceptance gated by replica availability
open_codes.rationale: The system refuses writes that cannot be committed to the minimum required number of replicas, rather than accepting data that may not be durably stored.

open_codes.label: Availability sacrifice for durability
open_codes.rationale: The document describes the adopted trade-off in which write availability is temporarily lost when sufficient copies cannot be created, preserving the promise not to lose accepted data.

open_codes.label: Durability evaluated at write acceptance
open_codes.rationale: Durability is tied to the moment a push, merge, edit, or repository creation is accepted; the relevant decision is how many copies are stored and where before making that promise.

open_codes.label: Write unavailability during replication shortfall
open_codes.rationale: When the minimum replica count cannot be achieved, the resulting effect is temporary unavailability for writes while durability is maintained.

open_codes.label: Three-phase commit protocol
open_codes.rationale: The system uses three-phase commit to update distant replicas while coordinating changes across them, accepting the cost of multiple network round-trips for replica consistency.

open_codes.label: Replica-based distributed locking
open_codes.rationale: Replicas are additionally used as a distributed lock so that database updates occur in the correct order.

open_codes.label: Four-round-trip replica update
open_codes.rationale: The combined commit and locking approach requires four round-trips to distant replicas, creating a measurable communication cost.

open_codes.label: Network-wait work overlap
open_codes.rationale: The coordinator performs other work while communication is in progress, such as acquiring one replica lock while another replica computes a checksum and the coordinator reads from the database.

open_codes.label: Distant-replica latency budget
open_codes.rationale: The design is constrained by the substantial latency of network round-trips to distant replicas, with a continental-US round-trip taking approximately 60–80 milliseconds and consuming the available time budget.

open_codes.label: Three-way repository replication
open_codes.rationale: Each repository is replicated on three servers so an up-to-date replica remains available when an individual server crashes or provides degraded service.

open_codes.label: Failure-aware request routing
open_codes.rationale: Spokes detects unavailable or degraded file servers and routes requests around them, using replication to preserve availability despite individual component failures.

open_codes.label: Combined heartbeat and real-traffic health detection
open_codes.rationale: Spokes uses both heartbeats and failures observed while processing real application traffic to identify file-server problems.

open_codes.label: Heartbeat-only health detection
open_codes.rationale: Relying solely on periodic heartbeats is rejected because heartbeats react too slowly at the system’s request volume and test only limited functionality, missing failures such as corrupt Git binaries, stalled disks, or failing authenticated operations.
