open_codes.label: Three-consecutive-request failure threshold
open_codes.rationale: Spokes marks a node offline only after three requests fail in a row, filtering occasional legitimate application-level failures such as deleted-branch reads or unauthorized pushes.

open_codes.label: False-positive node eviction
open_codes.rationale: The threshold can temporarily mark a healthy node offline when three requests fail by chance, but the document reports that this occurs infrequently and has a small availability penalty.

open_codes.label: Multi-replica repository storage
open_codes.rationale: Spokes stores several copies of each Git repository on different servers so repository data can be distributed across replicas and remain available for serving requests.

open_codes.label: Orchestrated push fan-out
open_codes.rationale: An orchestrator distributes each pushed packfile and reference transaction to every repository instance, ensuring that all replicas receive the push.

open_codes.label: Three-phase commit for reference transactions
open_codes.rationale: Spokes applies 3PC to the smaller reference transaction and accepts a push only when a majority of nodes acknowledge it, providing consensus for publication of the changes.

open_codes.label: Unsynchronized packfile distribution
open_codes.rationale: Packfiles are fanned out to all hosts without consensus synchronization because pushed objects are not reachable until the references are updated.

open_codes.label: Git reference-transaction locking
open_codes.rationale: The design uses Git's ability to prepare a reference transaction by locking the reference, verifying its expected value, and holding the lock until commit or abort.

open_codes.label: Single-replica read routing
open_codes.rationale: Once pushes are synchronized across replicas, fetches and clones can be routed to any one replica rather than requiring coordinated reads across nodes.

open_codes.label: Fully synchronized repository replicas
open_codes.rationale: The described design results in every replica being up to date after a push, which enables safe reads from any individual replica.

open_codes.label: Packfile-level application replication
open_codes.rationale: Spokes replicates Git data at the packfile level rather than distributing or modifying Git itself, preserving compatibility with Git's repository and packfile behavior.

open_codes.label: Git-level distribution
open_codes.rationale: The architecture explicitly avoids distributing Git itself, choosing packfile-level replication instead to avoid maintaining a distributed Git implementation.

open_codes.label: Plain Git repositories on local NVMe disks
open_codes.rationale: Spokes stores repositories in their native Git format on local NVMe drives to support random packfile reads, fast Git operations, and efficient clones.

open_codes.label: Git implementation fork for unusual repositories
open_codes.rationale: The approach avoids maintaining a fork of Git capable of operating on unusual repositories, allowing the team to build a product on top of Git instead.

open_codes.label: Fully consistent replica synchronization
open_codes.rationale: Spokes keeps all replicated copies consistently in sync because Git clients and CI workflows require a commit to be immediately readable after it is pushed or fetched.

open_codes.label: Eventual-consistency repository views
open_codes.rationale: The document describes eventual consistency as unsuitable for Git repositories because missing a newly pushed commit creates sharp edges for clients, backend operations, CI, and user experience.

open_codes.label: Replica-consistency complexity cost
open_codes.rationale: Maintaining fully synchronized copies imposes a very high system complexity cost, identified as the price of avoiding eventual-consistency failures.

open_codes.label: Simple storage-system architecture
open_codes.rationale: Continuity is explicitly designed as a simple system because the team considers simplicity necessary for operability at scale, rather than adding operationally complex storage components.

open_codes.label: S3-compatible object storage for the write-ahead log
open_codes.rationale: The system stores its WAL in S3-compatible object storage, runs on S3 in production, and preserves deployment flexibility across cloud providers instead of depending on a proprietary storage service.

open_codes.label: Durable push acknowledgement
open_codes.rationale: A push is not acknowledged until its WAL entry has been fully persisted, prioritizing durability and preventing clients from receiving success before the server has safely recorded the push.

open_codes.label: Separate object storage for each pushed packfile
open_codes.rationale: Each push is stored as a separate object, while the pushed packfile is written to local disk and uploaded to object storage concurrently; this defines the durable ingestion path for repository updates.

open_codes.label: WAL-indexed reference publication
open_codes.rationale: A push becomes visible only after its reference transaction is prepared on a local repository and a pointer to the WAL entry is recorded in the WAL index object, enforcing ordered and linearizable publication rather than exposing merely uploaded WAL data.

open_codes.label: Batched object-storage writes
open_codes.rationale: The implementation avoids one S3 write per push and uses carefully tuned batching to remove S3 PUT latency as a hard push-throughput limit in busy repositories.

open_codes.label: Single-local-repository synchronization
open_codes.rationale: Reference transactions are synchronized with one local repository instead of a quorum of replicas, reducing coordination overhead while supporting push ingestion at disk speed.

open_codes.label: Normal Git repository on local NVMe storage
open_codes.rationale: Continuity retains a standard Git repository on a very fast NVMe drive, reusing the upstream Git client and its optimizations rather than implementing a specialized Git-compatible storage layer.
